A.biggest_strength: An exceptionally intuitive, color-coded unified formula (ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN) paired with an interactive visual byte-stream model that shows moving TCB pointers (SND.NXT and RCV.NXT) and byte-state progression (sent vs acknowledged).
A.biggest_weakness: The sequence numbers and payload length are fixed constants (1000, 5000, and 5 bytes), without an option for the user to input custom values or toggle relative numbering.

B.biggest_strength: Interactive parameter controls allowing students to enter custom client/server ISNs and payload lengths, generate cryptographic random ISNs, and toggle relative sequence numbering like Wireshark.
B.biggest_weakness: Severely broken responsive layout on mobile screens, where hardcoding a 480px min-width on the SVG causes the entire server lifeline, its state badges, and incoming arrow heads to clip off-screen.
factual_errors: Informal phrasing in Step 3 stating 'The segment has no payload, so it uses no sequence number'—the segment does carry a 32-bit sequence number header field; it simply consumes zero sequence space.

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the clear winner because it actually visualizes the underlying mechanism of TCP sequence numbers rather than just displaying numbers in text boxes. By mapping sequence numbers to discrete byte-stream cells with sliding TCB pointers (SND.NXT and RCV.NXT) and uniting every calculation under the color-coded formula ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN, Page A provides immediate pedagogical clarity for networking students. In addition, Page A features outstanding depth with a real Linux kernel packet capture comparison, and its adaptive dual-viewBox layout renders flawlessly on mobile screens, whereas Page B's diagram cuts off the server lifeline on mobile devices.
